records.title: RAG in a Trenchcoat: When Minimal Memory Is Enough for Agentic Systems, and When It Isn't
records.abstract: Agentic memory research has accumulated extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we found that almost none of those primitives earn their cost in our tested memory benchmarks: we show this with BRIDGE, a deliberately minimal RAG memory with chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering, which reaches parity within bootstrap CI with the prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points at matched reader. It runs at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens per query, using a single LLM call for each ingestion or query. We argue that this parity is itself the result: standard benchmarks score what memory retrieves, not what memory enables when the agent acts. To test the latter, we introduce five adversarial probes (Rule Application +-, Pattern Induction Style / Procedural, Dynamic Multiturn) judged at generation time by a cross vendor verification chain, where each query can only be solved by applying a remembered rule or pattern it never mentions. Across 5 probes x 20 scenarios, no architecture wins universally: atomic fact extractors (LangMem) win rule application, while BRIDGE's block-summary memory wins pattern induction. This result holds across four domains, three graders, and three reader families. Each design fails where the other wins, for reasons a recall benchmark cannot see: atomic-fact extractors discard the form a demonstrated pattern takes, while block-summary memory retrieves the rule but the reader does not act on it, a gap that presenting the rule more prominently largely closes. What separates memory designs is not what they retrieve but what they enable an agent to do, and that is what agentic memory should be evaluated on.
records.comments: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), Main Conference

records.title: Learning In-Context Adaptivity for LLMs through Continual Gameplay
records.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in long-horizon tasks where they must explore, gather experience, and adapt their decisions accordingly. We name this capability in-context adaptivity: improving decisions across episodes from experience accumulated in context. We propose to evaluate it in repeated imperfect-information games against unknown opponents. In these games, fixed game-theoretically optimal policies cannot achieve maximum reward, whereas adapting to the opponent increases returns across games. We design a paired protocol that evaluates each agent with and without memory under identical conditions to isolate experience gain from single-game skill. Evaluation shows that memory brings little performance gain for open-weight models and inconsistent gains for frontier models. Our analysis of the agents' summaries and actions identifies a memory-doing gap in which models accurately record opponent tendencies yet rarely depart from default play. To close this gap, we construct a pool of exploitable opponents and post-train Qwen3.5-9B with supervised fine-tuning followed by trajectory-level reinforcement learning. We optimize full-match return across context segments so summary generation and action selection are trained together. On unseen opponents, our 9B RL policy doubles experience gain over supervised fine-tuning in Leduc Hold'em and increases it fivefold in No-Limit Hold'em. Across 35 opponents, our policy matches or surpasses frontier models, generalizes beyond its training horizon, and retains most of its gain on summaries from frontier models.

records.title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
records.abstract: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.

records.title: DailyBrick: Language-Guided Synthesis of Brick Assembly Instructions
records.abstract: Generating a LEGO model from a user request is more than a plausible 3D shape generation. LEGO models require physical support per brick, and each brick should be placed unblocked. Current methods address this issue by training an expert large language model. We reduce the problem of generating extremely long context on all brick connections to that of writing a program that builds LEGO models like a human, considering each intermediate step could be executed. We introduce DailyBrick , a multi-stage agentic system that produces a LEGO model together with a brick-by-brick assembly instruction for human building and robot assembly. We design a multi-stage harness with roles to help LLMs generate more effectively. A versioned construction SDK compiles multi-level decisions, from semantic subparts to individual bricks, into canonical operations. An external Meta-Reviewer agent replays and inspects the generated package, verifies the model and its construction process, identifies failures, traces them to the responsible stage, and routes them to bounded repairs or to editable candidates for later skill or tool updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DailyBrick generates LEGO models based on simple user requests better than recent agentic systems, and show its utility in downstream applications such as robot manipulations on model assembly from instructions and brick sets (https://spatialagentlab.github.io/DailyBrick.github.io/).

records.title: Great Listeners, Poor Decision-Makers: Rethinking Agentic Audio AI
records.abstract: Audio artificial intelligence (AI) now recognizes speech, sounds, and music remarkably well, yet voice agents still act when they should not: they execute commands addressed to others, act on misheard content, and commit before the user finishes speaking. This position article argues that the bottleneck in agentic audio AI has shifted from recognition to decision-making. We propose a reference architecture with an explicit decision layer, separate from perception and reasoning, that chooses whether to act, wait, ask, or remain silent from evidence on addressedness, speaker identity, content confidence, tool reliability, utterance completeness, and action risk. We motivate the design through six recurring decision failures and a decision-theoretic argument that transcript confidence alone is insufficient to justify an action. We implement the layer with fuzzy inference, evolutionary optimization, and sequential decision-making, and evaluate it through simulations, ablations, and recorded audio, including egocentric recordings. Addressedness and speaker evidence matter most, risk-aware gating suppresses costly errors, and well-tuned policies perform similarly, with fuzzy gates more robust to overconfident addressedness estimates. On recorded audio, explicit gating cuts executed side talk from 41\% to 7--10\% while serving 83--85\% of valid requests under successful clarification, outperforming prompting-based baselines. These results support explicit action gating as an architectural requirement for reliable voice agents.

records.title: RoboTeam: Benchmarking Vision-Based Multi-Agent Control of Many Robot Arms in Real Time
records.abstract: Multimodal agents can now control robot arms by calling tools and writing code. Existing benchmarks fall short in three ways: most test one or two arms on short tasks, many pause the world while the agent thinks, and many give it ground-truth object positions. We present RoboTeam, a simulated benchmark where agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone. Its 36 tasks are long jobs that the arms must do together, such as passing timbers or building a picture from hundreds of cubes. We start from the most flexible agent system, the adaptive system, where one agent decides when to fork delegates. With it, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 tasks, and four other models at most 3. But at a high price: a typical task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. We then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized. All four complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. Even so, no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. RoboTeam measures these limits where earlier benchmarks cannot: long multi-arm jobs, camera images only, and a world that never pauses.

records.title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness
records.abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.

records.title: Securing and Auditing Long-Horizon LLM Agents: State-Transfer Auditing and Controls in the Agent Harness
records.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents across codebases, web browsers, and enterprise infrastructure rely on an execution harness to move state between the working context, session history, persistent memory, and external environment. While conventional execution traces log model prompts and tool calls, critical security and reliability failures occur during state transfers: a transfer can admit unchecked content (indirect prompt injections, unverified memory writes), rewrite state lossily (context compaction dropping user constraints, memory consolidation stripping source authority), or restore state incompletely (workspace rollbacks leaving aborted KV state active on the inference server). Because current traces omit what crosses these boundaries, failure attribution and runtime monitors fail on multi-step trajectories. We present a state-transfer audit architecture for the agent harness. At each transfer boundary, we define an audit point specifying the minimal hash-chained record the harness emits, separating low-overhead deterministic checks from model-based semantic checks and binding internal context, memory, and inference-server cache state to external actions. We show that the same transfer records required for causal failure attribution supply the durable state needed by runtime security controls, including least-privilege capabilities, replay-resistant authorization outside the prompt, information flow control, obligation monitors, and transactional recovery across multi-agent and infrastructure pipelines. Finally, we analyze multimodal GUI adaptations and implement and evaluate a reference harness middleware across 240 multi-step fault-injection trajectories, showing that transfer records localize root causes and catch cross-transfer violations missed by lifecycle and tool-only logs at microsecond deterministic overhead.

records.title: Reliability by Architecture: Agentic Workflows for Validated Multi-Physics Simulation from Natural Language
records.abstract: Preparing, executing, and validating strongly coupled multi-physics simulations require expert time. Agentic workflows use large language models (LLMs) to coordinate them from natural-language descriptions, but reliability requires checks of physical consistency and fidelity to the problem description. Our agentic harness implements explicit task allocation: LLMs interpret user requests and simulator diagnostics, generate input components not covered by predefined construction rules, and propose repairs, while deterministic routines construct supported components and check inputs, edits, and results. We evaluate CO2-storage problems using the multi-physics simulator GEOS, from compositional flow to flow-poromechanics with frictional fault contact. In 80 attempts on two flow problems, grounding raises the proportion of structurally valid inputs from 5/20 to 20/20, but acceptance reaches 20/20 only with complete rule-based input preparation. With identical inputs, local repairs correct three seeded defects while preserving valid inputs. Supporting tests identify simulations passing physics checks despite differing from the problem description or reference results.

records.title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
records.abstract: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.
records.comments: 18 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Work in progress: benchmark design and protocol; results to be added in a later version

records.title: ViStep-RL: Stepwise Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Visual Agents
records.abstract: Long-horizon visual agents must do more than inspect images: they must turn observations into evidence that remains usable as a task unfolds. Existing active-perception methods teach agents where and how to look, while a final-answer reward gives little structure for deciding which observations satisfy dependent subgoals or should be retained for later use. We present ViStep-RL (Visual Stepwise Reinforcement Learning), which models execution as a dependency-linked graph of evidence-bearing subgoals. A verifier tracks which subgoals are supported by valid evidence, and changes in graph potential provide a net-progress learning signal; an active memory protocol preserves evidence across turns and links retrieval to downstream use. On ViInteract, ViStep-RL reaches 60.0% strict completion with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, compared with 10.0% for the base model and 46.5% after supervised fine-tuning. Controlled studies show that incremental task-state rewards outperform cumulative rewards by 3.2 points, while active evidence writing improves strict completion by 7.75 points over automatic writing. Under a common interaction framework, the task-trained ViStep-RL policy achieves 59.5% answer accuracy, 24.0 points above the strongest of six general-purpose reference models. Held-out episodes confirm the gain at both Qwen scales, and gains extend to three external visual reasoning benchmarks.

records.title: Depth Before Breadth: Reverse-to-Forward Curriculum with Advantage Decomposition for LLM Agent
records.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, learning from sparse terminal rewards makes credit assignment and exploration difficult. We approach these challenges through a policy-induced capability region, the set of states from which the current policy can reliably complete a task. Near its boundary, an agent may need only a few actions to reach a more solvable state, even when the goal remains distant. This reduces long-horizon learning to two coupled subproblems of reaching that state and completing the task from there. We address them with paired advantages and a progressive reverse-to-forward curriculum. The advantages provide separate signals for reaching more solvable states and completing the task from them, while the curriculum expands the capability region backward along successful reference trajectories and then into off-reference states through on-policy exploration. On ALFWorld and WebShop, our method outperforms competitive agentic RL methods at both model scales, achieving success rates of 90.1%/96.1% and 80.2%/82.6% with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, respectively.

records.title: Vibe-Trading: Towards Agent-Native Trading
records.abstract: Existing AI agents can retrieve information, call tools, run experiments, and produce multi-step outputs. Yet most are built around relatively static workflows and struggle to preserve reliable state as the environment changes. Financial trading makes this limitation especially consequential: prices, news, market conditions, portfolio positions, and available capital evolve continuously. A result is useful only when it remains tied to the correct time, data snapshot, and execution context. We present Vibe-Trading, a comprehensive agent-native trading framework and all-in-one workspace for building, evaluating, and evolving agents for financial trading. It unifies market research, financial data, strategy generation, backtesting, portfolio analysis, paper trading, multi-agent collaboration, and optional broker execution. Its central contribution is an architecture that keeps results, evidence, research history, and trading authority connected throughout the research-to-action process. Each result retains its source, temporal scope, configuration, and producing run. Shared evidence grounding enables verification, versioned research records support reproducible continuation, and an explicit authority gate separates strategy research from live execution. Together, these designs provide a practical foundation for trading agents whose results can be traced, reproduced, and acted on only under explicit authority.
records.comments: Technical report. 16 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Code: https://github.com/HKUDS/Vibe-Trading

records.title: Resolution as Attention for Efficient Agent Memory Perception
records.abstract: LLM-based agents accumulate extensive interaction histories when solving complex, long-horizon tasks, making efficient memory management critical to their performance and scalability. While existing memory management methods primarily focus on what to retain or retrieve, they often overlook how much perceptual detail should be allocated to individual past interactions. We posit that effective agent memory depends not only on the information preserved, but also on the granularity at which each past interaction is perceived. Motivated by this insight, we propose Resolution as Attention (RAA), a memory perception mechanism that uses visual resolution as a means of attention allocation across interaction histories. RAA renders past interactions as images and dynamically adjusts their resolution at every step according to their relevance to the agent's upcoming decision, preserving fine-grained information for critical interactions while reducing visual-token consumption for less relevant ones. To adaptively determine the perceptual fidelity of each interaction, we train a lightweight relevance estimator with teacher-model guidance and further optimize it to preserve the agent's decision consistency at a reduced visual-token cost. Experiments across multiple tasks and backbones show that RAA reduces token consumption by over 50% without compromising task performance. Moreover, RAA can be integrated as a plug-in perception layer with existing memory management methods, yielding further token savings and revealing adaptive perception as a complementary dimension of agent memory.

records.title: RoboBuilder: Agentic Robot Co-Design with Real-world Video Feedback in the Loop
records.abstract: Can AI agents design robots that work in the real world? We introduce RoboBuilder, a benchmark in which coding agents co-design a robot's hardware and program from standard parts, motors and a custom 3D-printed part, and every design that passes in simulation is built and tested on a physical course. Simulation alone is not enough: under public part data, none of 15 initial passing designs crossed the real course, so an agent learns the simulator from measurements it requests and videos of real runs. Across four frontier coding agents, ten obstacles at three difficulty levels, 16,427 simulations of 12,774 distinct robots and 135 physical robots built in an estimated 240 hours, agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and invent mechanisms our search baselines do not reach, but falter at harder levels, when one robot must cross every obstacle, and in the real world, where 66% of simulated passes hold across all levels. Closing the loop helps: shown a video of its real failure, an agent redesigns the robot, sometimes correcting its simulator, and removes 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures. RoboBuilder measures progress toward agents that engineer real machines. Project Page: https://ghadinehme.com/robobuilder.github.io/

records.title: Semantic Context Handoff with On-Demand Evidence for Long-Horizon Agents
records.abstract: Traditional long-horizon LLM agents often hand off context through full-history prompting, retaining all previous action--observation interactions. As execution proceeds, this history keeps growing, increasing inference cost and potentially degrading accuracy. Existing methods control this growth by preserving compact conclusions while removing earlier observations, but doing so can discard evidence that later becomes relevant. We introduce Semantic Context Handoff (SCH), whose central abstraction is state--evidence separation: a compact semantic state carries the agent's current interpretation, while supporting action--observation evidence remains separately addressable and can re-enter context when later execution makes it relevant, without separate summarization or retrieval-model calls. Empirically, SCH improves long-horizon agent performance while substantially reducing context cost. In a controlled 150-task SWE-bench study, SCH's evidence recovery improves Pass@1 from $80.0\%$ to $86.9\%$ at essentially unchanged token use and execution time. In the complete-system comparison, SCH achieves 86.9% Pass@1 while using 43% fewer tokens and 41% less wall-clock time than the strongest baseline by task performance. Across models and benchmarks, SCH consistently reduces token use relative to full-history prompting while remaining competitive with or improving upon the evaluated baselines. Trajectory analysis confirms that SCH recovers evidence from substantially earlier parts of the interaction history rather than merely preserving a recent context window.

records.title: 3D GameDev Arena: Benchmarking Coding Agents That Plan, Build, and Playtest extreme Long-Horizon Browser Games
records.abstract: Coding agents now resolve repository issues and generate compact playable games, but whether they can build a large 3D game from scratch remains open. Such games tightly couple mechanics, scenes, assets, and interaction logic, and their quality rests on player enjoyment, which existing benchmarks rarely assess. Thus, we introduce 3D GameDev Arena, a first extreme long-horizon benchmark of 108 from-scratch game-development tasks across 14 genres. Given only a text specification and UI/UX reference images, a fully automated plan--implement--test--repair pipeline builds each task into a self-contained browser game. Runs average $\sim$1,000 LLM calls ; the longest uses 14,407 calls, 2.13B tokens, and 608 assets. Evaluation spans (1) objective code-level functional acceptance against the game specification, (2) agent-based QA and playtesting of 3D presentation and playability, and (3) blind pairwise Bradley-Terry human preference in a public arena. The preliminary findings indicate that long-horizon 3D game development remains far from solved, and code-level correctness alone does not dictate player preference. The public arena is hosted online.

records.title: SCAFFOLD: Toward Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport for Reusable LLM-Agent Skills
records.abstract: An agent skill that succeeded yesterday may be executable today without being justified for reuse today. Tests may cover only observable contract clauses, outcome oracles may be absent, evaluations may inherit the same erroneous specification, and permissions or dependencies may change between validation and invocation. We argue that the appropriate unit of prospective trust is a Warranted Reuse Claim (WRC): a defeasible, claim-specific authorization tied to a versioned skill, target context, evidence, assumptions, and identified defeaters. The paper sharpens this position through Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport (WPET), a proposed discipline for deciding which historical evidence remains admissible after context change. It distinguishes evidence admissibility from truth of the supported safety or effectiveness claim; states a conditional preservation result and its limits; specifies three-valued applicability and asymmetric context-transfer judgments; and illustrates how provenance dependence and policy-invalidating changes alter authorization. We explicitly relate the proposal to assurance cases, contracts, and skill-library maintenance rather than claiming novelty for their ingredients. A falsifiable longitudinal evaluation would compare WRC-guided policies with strong version-aware baselines at matched coverage, utility, and review cost. This paper contributes a formalized problem statement, testable design obligations, and reporting protocol, not an implemented verifier, empirical superiority result, or proof of universal agent safety.

records.title: Think Offline, Act in Real Time: Self-Improving Visual Game Agents through Code
records.abstract: Pre-trained models can read screens and reason about games, yet on an unfamiliar game, an agent still has to learn to play. We ask how an agent can self-improve on such a game from a few of its own attempts, in real-time visual games where the agent sees only the screen and the game keeps running while the agent thinks. We study two kinds of policy that can carry this improvement. In model as policy, a model selects actions during play; we adapt real-time chunking so that committed actions keep executing while the model reasons, and train a 2B controller for this interface. In code as policy, a model writes, tests, and revises a program between attempts, and the program acts during play. Across 170 GameWorld tasks, with at most eight one-minute executions per run, code as policy reaches 47.80% mean progress, against 30.90% for our trained controller, and leads in all five game categories. Improving the controller's weights on a single game, by contrast, yields only modest gains. These results favor letting a model think offline and storing what it learns in a program that acts in real time. Project repository: https://github.com/TabibitoQZP/SIGame

records.title: SceneAnything: Agentic Reconstruction of Large-Scale Mesh Scenes from a Single Video
records.abstract: Reconstructing an editable 3D scene from video requires matching visible structure while plausibly completing unseen surfaces. Agents can write scene-construction programs, but direct reconstruction attempts often produce errors in layout, scale, and lighting. We introduce SceneAnything, an automated system for reconstructing mesh scenes from real and generated videos, enabling text-to-scene construction when paired with video generation. A software harness coordinates agents, pretrained vision models, and graphics tools through an explicit reconstruction protocol. Shared camera, depth, and segmentation estimates ground component construction: a scene-owner agent plans the environment and briefs authors, who write parameterized Blender programs. A visibility- and fit-based level-of-detail rule selects the construction level, while unseen regions are completed and marked as inferred. Assembled scenes use fitted lighting and supported motion, and revisions undergo programmatic checks and independent visual comparisons. Accepted programs and lessons are reused across scenes. We evaluate on 100 scenes; subset comparisons show improved original-view fidelity over direct-agent reconstruction and higher novel-view content similarity than the compared video-to-3D methods. We will release the harness, agent instructions, reusable libraries, and scenes.

records.title: HabitusMem: Belief Memory over Evolving User Preferences for LLM Agents
records.abstract: Personalized LLM agents must act on a user's current preferences, which change across interactions and are rarely stated in full. Existing memory systems store and retrieve content from the interaction history and leave the agent to work out which preferences still hold and where they apply. Such content does not indicate whether a preference is still current or where it applies, so agents often act on outdated or misapplied preferences. We instead treat memory as the assistant's belief about the user. Following Bourdieu's account of habitus as durable but revisable dispositions, we model the user as a latent preference state that every interaction, including the current request, both reveals and updates. The belief summarizes what the history supports about this state, and memory consists of the individual beliefs that bear on the agent's current decision, each with its evidence, scope, and status. We implement this view in HabitusMem, a trained writer that states these beliefs as text records for a frozen agent. Across two agent families, HabitusMem achieves the best results among memory systems on both PersonaMem-v2 and VitaBench 2.0. Controlled analyses show that learned request conditioning drives the answering gain, while auxiliary training tasks improve tool use.

records.title: WeightCode: Installing New Capabilities into Neural Networks via Weight-Space Programming
records.abstract: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.
records.comments: 26 pages, 11 figures, including appendix. Code: https://github.com/Gen-Verse/WeightCode

records.title: How Feedback-Free Self-Evolution Reshapes Agent Skills: A Systematic Study
records.abstract: Agent skills are documents in which experts write down procedural knowledge, and models increasingly maintain them by rewriting them without feedback. Such rewriting could adapt a skill to the model that uses it or erode the expert knowledge that makes it useful, yet how skills evolve under this feedback-free self-evolution has not been studied. We let models rewrite expert skills round after round without any task, run or judgment and run agents built on the same models with the rewritten skills. Our experiments show that the skills lose value rather than improve, as every model we test performs worse with them on every benchmark, by 15 points on average on SkillsBench after thirty rounds. Sampling each model's prior with skills it writes from the topic alone, we find that rewriting pulls skills toward this prior and gives up first the knowledge outside it. Putting this knowledge back recovers much of the lost pass rate, so an expert's skill is valuable largely for what the model does not write on its own. Building on this insight, SkillDiff marks this knowledge in place and raises the pass rate on SkillsBench by 4.8 points on average without feedback or any change to the skill's text. Project repository: https://github.com/LitaoGuo/How-Self-Evolution-Reshapes-Skills.

records.title: DACA: Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent for Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding
records.abstract: 3D visual grounding (3D-VG) is a task that bridges the natural language and 3D space, serving as a foundational capability for embodied intelligence and human-computer interaction. Although recent 3D-VG agents overcome the reliance on pre-processed 3D point clouds, they essentially employ a unidirectional, pipeline-style tool-calling architecture. This architecture separates semantic understanding from geometric reconstruction, leading to error accumulation and an inability to autonomously recover from failures. To address this flaw, this paper proposes the Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent (DACA), which reinterprets 3D-VG as a semantic-geometric dual-anchor collaborative reasoning paradigm. DACA comprises two complementary specialized tools: the semantic anchor tool holds the visual semantic features of the target and achieves efficient target tracking via optical flow and VLM local verification; the geometric anchor tool holds the 3D spatial geometric features of the target and performs global spatial reasoning via voxelization and multi-keypoint projection. The two components exchange information bidirectionally via a standardized tool call protocol, autonomously deciding on the next perception-action step to form a closed-loop optimization. Experiments on the ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks demonstrate that zero-shot DACA achieves an overall Acc@0.25 of 73.6\% on ScanRefer and 70.4\% overall accuracy on Nr3D, far surpassing the latest zero-shot 3D-VG methods. The code and models are available at https://github.com/liujia99/DACA

records.title: Context as a Resource
records.abstract: Managing concurrent tasks across separate agent sessions quickly exhausts human attention, motivating always-on personal agents behind a single continuous interface. Yet when every context shares identical frozen backbone weights, funneling interleaved dialogues and external events into one linear session induces cross-topic constraint bleed and head-of-line stalling. Conversely, router-ticket hierarchies incur lossy prose handoffs, heavy routing overhead, and blind merges - collapsing true-conflict repository merges to a 33.3% three-run mean despite high isolated branch passes. Rather than scheduling anthropomorphic roles, we introduce ClonAct, a routerless architecture that virtualizes context blocks directly through a pluggable single-pass non-generative Context MMU, in-place Context Cells, a footprint-aware Synaptic Bus with an isolated trial merge gate, and a wave-flushed Shared Trunk. Across three programmatic multi-stream benchmarks and three model families, our portable trial merge gate lifts true-conflict merges to 63.3%, while ClonAct's routerless virtualization attains this ceiling with 45.9% fewer prompt tokens and prevents compact-model router collapse. Under continuous surge streams, ClonAct matches top completion (95.0%) with the lowest median wait and zero timed-out status checks.

records.title: JARVIS: An Agent That Designs, Builds, and Tests Circuit Boards on Its Own
records.abstract: Power electronics is central to the energy transition, but developing new hardware still relies on human-led design, fabrication, testing, and iteration. We present JARVIS, an embodied AI agent that autonomously closes this loop for circuit boards. JARVIS maintains machine-specific capabilities and constraints, scans its workspace using a robot-mounted 3D scanner, and constructs an executable digital twin in which it rehearses robot motions, fabrication steps, and circuit behavior before consuming materials. A single text instruction initiates the physical experiment. Using unmodified desktop equipment, the agent coordinates a robot arm, a PCB printer that deposits conductive silver ink and solder paste, and a pick-and-place machine. It verifies progress using cameras and sensors, then tests the fabricated circuit with an OPAL-RT real-time simulator and an oscilloscope. Based on the measurements, JARVIS diagnoses deviations from the design and generates a revised design in KiCad for subsequent rehearsal. In a demonstration involving a 60 Hz notch filter for grid-connected converter sensing, JARVIS completed a first-run experiment in 2 h 39 min without human intervention, achieving 50.6 dB attenuation at 60 Hz. Its digital-twin rehearsal identified five issues before fabrication, including a test criterion that would have incorrectly rejected a functioning board. During execution, the agent also resolved encountered faults autonomously. These results demonstrate an integrated agent-driven workflow for physical design, fabrication, measurement, and iterative improvement of power-electronic circuitry. To our knowledge, JARVIS is the first system in power electronics in which an agent closes the physical design-build-test-learn loop for circuit boards.

records.title: TRACE: Attribute Execution for Sequential Image Editing
records.abstract: Given an image and successive user instructions, sequential image editing should return an updated image that satisfies each new request and preserves earlier requirements that remain active. This lets users develop a result without repeatedly restating or repairing their decisions. The difficulty is that a retrieved image can contain a valid color on an obsolete surface, while the current image may lack the newly requested material. Neither reference selection nor a precise object mask alone specifies how to reconcile attributes occupying the same region. We present TRACE, which separates the continuing attribute from its visual carrier and prioritizes local appearance operations under complete-request checks. Active-goal binding identifies what should persist, carrier selection supplies suitable current or newly generated pixels, and tonal calibration reduces tinting near highlights and shadows. Experiments across frozen editors, independent visual readers, new source images, and complete sequential benchmarks support joint color-material recovery and show how local execution preserves the surrounding scene.
